Title: How AI App Builders Leak Their Own Credentials
Context: Executive summary: AI app builders give generated apps owner-level access The Orca Research Pod found the same architectural mistake in multiple independent AI app builder...
Full Text:
Executive summary: AI app builders give generated apps owner-level access

The Orca Research Pod found the same architectural mistake in multiple independent AI app builder platforms. Code the platform generates inherits the authority of the build environment.

These platforms build the app inside their own trust boundary and never take it back out. As a result, the generated app gets owner-level authority over the developer’s connected accounts and backend. The developer never granted that authority, can’t see it and can’t revoke it.

Key findings

Across several platforms, we confirmed that generated applications could do the following. In some cases, so could anonymous visitors to those apps.

Act as the account owner on connected third-party services

Read live database credentials belonging to other customers

Call privileged backend functions that bypass row-level security entirely

Reach platform secrets from inside the build sandbox

In none of these cases did the developer misconfigure anything. The authority is there by default, in the environment, before the first line of application code is written.

What is ambient authority in AI app builders?

Ambient authority is privilege that sits in the surrounding environment instead of being granted to a specific caller for a specific purpose.

An AI app builder has to be powerful to be useful. To scaffold a working application, it needs to write files, install dependencies, provision a database, commit to your repository and read the services you connected. So the platform gives its build environment broad authority over your accounts.

Then it puts your application in that same environment. Nothing separates the two. The credential the agent used to build the app is still there when the app runs, and the app can read it just as easily as the agent could.

The pattern isn’t one vendor’s bug. It keeps showing up because every builder faces the same design pressure:

Platform

What the generated app is handed

A major AI app builder

A plaintext environment variable that acts as a bearer credential for the account owner on every connected third-party service

A major AI app builder

A live platform session token in the agent’s environment, plus an unauthenticated internal LLM proxy billing the vendor’s own account

A generated backend

Supabase edge functions holding a service-role key, with the JWT gateway defaulted off

A build sandbox

Platform secrets readable by any process running inside it

Three ways AI app builders leak credentials in the wild

One environment variable exposes every connected service

On a major AI app builder, a single plaintext environment variable is present in every project. It authorizes the caller as the account owner across the account’s connected services: GitHub, Gmail, Slack and Drive. The GitHub connector’s scope is full repository access, read and write, private repositories included.

The platform’s AI agent isn’t involved at any point, and that matters more than it first appears. Undocumented endpoints return each connector’s raw OAuth access token, which then works directly against GitHub or Google. No request passes through the platform, so the platform’s logging, rate limiting and revocation never see the traffic.

Three properties make this worse than a typical leaked secret:

Collaborators inherit it. Any project collaborator gets the token through the shared shell, with no planted code and no remix. Revoking the invitation doesn’t revoke tokens they’ve already taken.

The token is portable and long-lived. It’s signed, not encrypted, so anyone holding it can read its claims. Replayed from an unrelated laptop, it still returned the account’s data.

The platform’s scanner misses it. The platform’s own security scanner reports code that exfiltrates the variable as clean. The control users trust to tell them a project is safe says it’s safe.

An unprotected API endpoint leaks database credentials across tenants

At another builder, which we’re not naming, a single API endpoint returned any project’s database integration to any logged-in user of the platform. That included a live database key and the full project configuration. Nothing checked that the caller owned the project, and project IDs were small sequential integers.

Counting through one ID range returned live credentials for thousands of projects across dozens of organizations. That included projects hosted in customers’ own third-party database accounts. The keys are genuine and long-lived. We confirmed cross-tenant reads against multiple unrelated tenants. We also reproduced the issue on a project created during testing, so new projects were affected too.

Where row-level security wasn’t configured, the credentials led straight to the data behind them. Most sampled databases also had email auto-confirm and open signup turned on. An attacker with a leaked key could register a confirmed account and reach everything the authenticated role can see, which is usually far more than the anonymous role.

AI-generated Supabase edge functions bypass row-level security

The third instance involves no platform defect at all. Nothing is broken on the platform’s side. The AI wrote the vulnerability and shipped it.

Ask a builder for an app with a database, and it generates Supabase edge functions to do the work. Many of those functions hold a service_role key, Supabase’s administrative credential, which bypasses row-level security entirely. One builder also ships them with the JWT gateway turned off, so the function answers anyone who calls it. The result is an unauthenticated endpoint holding a key that ignores every access control you configured.

Those defaults come from the generator, not Supabase. The pattern lasts because developers have no reason to suspect it. One developer recorded the belief in a source comment: “The Publishable Key is the successor to the anon key: it is public and safe for client-side code (Row-Level Security protects the data).”

That’s correct, and it matches Supabase’s own guidance. It’s also beside the point, because the app’s own service_role function goes straight around row-level security. The developer secured the front door of a house with no back wall.

This is why teams need to catch risky code before it reaches production, including code an AI agent wrote.

Why prompt injection defenses don’t stop AI app builder credential leaks

The obvious reading of any AI platform vulnerability is prompt injection. Here, it’s the wrong one.

We tried it. On a major AI app builder, the agent resisted every prompt injection attempt we made. Plain application code then walked straight past it, because the code didn’t need to persuade the agent of anything. It just read a variable.

Injection is one delivery route among many. The real defect is that the authority is ambient in the first place. It sits in the environment, where any code and any collaborator can reach it, and in one case any anonymous visitor too. Defenses placed at the agent don’t protect a credential that lives next to it.

That distinction decides where the fix has to go. Guardrails on the model aren’t a control over the environment.

How to secure apps built with AI app builders

Several of these issues were still unfixed when we wrote this. These steps don’t depend on a vendor fix:

Assume the generated app can reach every connected integration. Connect only the services a project needs, at the narrowest scope the builder will accept, and disconnect the rest. Identities with too much access are where this risk starts, so reduce identity-based cloud risk across these connections.

Rotate keys for any project built on these platforms. Treat platform-issued tokens as compromised if a project was ever shared, remixed or made public.

Turn on row-level security for every table, then check it. A table with RLS enabled but no policy isn’t a protected table.

Audit generated backend functions for service-role keys. Confirm each function authenticates its caller, and turn the JWT gateway on. Unauthenticated functions are effectively exposed APIs, so find and secure unmanaged APIs as part of the audit.

Inventory the pair, not just the app. The risk object is the generated application plus the managed database behind it. Neither half alone tells you what’s exposed, so find and protect sensitive data across your cloud behind every generated app.

Frequently asked questions about AI app builder security

Are AI app builders safe to use?

They can be. But this research shows that generated apps can inherit owner-level access to connected accounts by default, so scope integrations narrowly and audit what gets generated.

Does Supabase row-level security protect AI-generated apps?

Not if a generated edge function uses the service_role key, because that key bypasses RLS entirely.

Is this a prompt injection problem?

No. In our testing, plain application code read the credential directly without involving the agent.

How can Orca help secure AI-generated applications?

Orca’s unified cloud security platform brings the full AI footprint into a single risk model alongside your cloud context: the models and MCP servers teams connect, the code AI agents write and the applications AppGen platforms generate.

Orca also helps security teams uncover apps built with AI tools, so generated applications and the data behind them don’t sit outside security’s view. Because Orca sees those connections together, it can surface the issues that turn a generated app into a breach path: overprivileged identities and integrations, exposed secrets in code, unauthenticated APIs and sensitive data without the right protections. Orca then prioritizes them by what an attacker could actually reach. Teams can keep building with AI at full speed while security keeps pace, without adding agents or slowing developers down.

Title: Caught by Behavior: How Orca Sensor Exposed a Cloud Intrusion in Real Time
Context: From the exploited web app to the second wave, the attack raised Critical and High alerts in the customer’s Orca console as it unfolded, with the detections running in alert mode
Full Text:
Executive summary: Runtime behavior exposed what indicators missed

No known indicator flagged this attack. Orca Sensor did, in real time.

A CVE in a scanned package, a malware hash, a bad IP address or domain: known signals like these catch known threats. This intrusion brought none of them, so threat intelligence and CVE scanning had nothing to flag for what the attacker used. What gave it away was behavior.

Orca Sensor flagged the shell commands the exploited web app started, through its Node.js remote code execution (RCE) detections, and kept flagging the attacker’s activity as it spread. In total, 18 behavioral detections fired, spanning seven MITRE ATT&CK tactics, and none of them relied on a known hash, IP address, domain, or CVE. From the exploited web app to the second wave, the attack raised Critical and High alerts in the customer’s Orca console as it unfolded, with the detections running in alert mode.

Orca’s research team spotted the activity in the sensor data and proactively reached out to the customer to share the full picture of the attack and help their team scope and contain it.

Where known indicators go silent, behavior speaks

Orca Sensor is a lightweight eBPF sensor for runtime detection and response. It watches processes, files and network activity on hosts and in containers as they happen.

This attacker brought nothing known:

No hash to match. The binary they ran was not flagged by threat intelligence.

No IP or domain to match. Neither the domain the binary was downloaded from nor the external address used in a reverse shell attempt was flagged by threat intelligence.

No untrusted image. The containers they started used images from the company’s own private registry, so an image allowlist alone would not have blocked them.

No CVE to scan for. The activity matched a flaw in the web app that had no public CVE at the time.

What the attacker could not hide was behavior, and behavior is what the sensor watches.

Known signals like these only work once someone has already seen that attacker or that flaw. Behavior describes what an attacker does, and that is much harder to change. Attackers can swap their tools, servers and entry points, but the steps they need stay the same: run commands, look for credentials, ask the cloud metadata service for access, try to break out of containers, and set up a way back in.

That is why the detections that fired here were not written for this attacker or this flaw. They describe techniques, and they fired because the attacker used them. And runtime is where those steps happen, so the sensor sees what the attacker does, even when there is nothing known to match.

As more attackers turn to AI agents that tailor their tools to every target and find flaws no one has reported yet, every attack can look brand new. Their behavior is what still gives them away.

Attack timeline: From Node.js RCE to container escape and persistence

Code execution in the web app. A self-hosted web app built on Node.js, running as root, started a shell that ran system recon commands. Two Node.js RCE detections fired on that first command, and a third fired minutes later when the attacker dropped a script in /tmp and ran it. In this environment, these detections fired only on the attack, not on the app’s normal activity. Every later alert on that server traced back to the app’s own process.

Recon and secret hunting. Next, the sensor caught searches for SSH keys and cloud credential files, scans for etcd and the kubelet API, and requests to the cloud metadata service for the temporary credentials it can issue to a workload.

Moving into other services. The attacker then ran commands inside other application containers, among them base64-encoded Python scripts that collected environment variables and listed running processes. In several containers, they also ran a hidden binary from /tmp that deleted itself right after it started.

Breaking out to the host. The attacker started privileged containers that shared the host’s process namespace and mounted its filesystem, and used them to enter the host’s namespaces. On one host, they installed a copy of that binary under a disguised name, which then launched more privileged containers. They also tried to install system services to come back after a reboot.

A second wave. After a quiet period, new containers appeared on hosts that had not been touched before. They downloaded the attacker’s binary and ran it. The same kind of behavioral detections caught the new activity, from reverse shell attempts to fresh requests for cloud credentials.

Across the intrusion, 18 detections fired, spanning seven MITRE ATT&CK tactics:

Tactic

What the sensor caught

Execution

A web app starting shells that ran recon commands, a script dropped in /tmp and run, base64-encoded Python scripts, reverse shell attempts

Discovery

Commands checking which user was running inside a container, and connections probing internal services such as etcd, to map what else could be reached

Credential access

Searches for SSH keys and cloud credential files, running an application’s own code to pull its stored secrets, requests to the cloud metadata service

Privilege escalation

Entering the host’s namespaces and starting privileged containers

Defense evasion

Hidden files in /tmp and a binary named like a kernel process that deleted itself right after it started, both ways to stay out of sight on disk

Persistence

Privileged containers set to restart automatically, and attempts to enable system services from inside a container, all ways to keep or regain access

Lateral movement

Connections from shells and scripts inside containers to the kubelet API on several hosts, probing for a way to reach other workloads

How process tree context tied every alert to the attacker

The alerts carried the command line and the process tree behind each event, along with the host and the Linux user. For containers, they also carried the container name, image, and registry, and whether the container was privileged. That context is what turned separate alerts into one story. A credential search or a request to the metadata service did not stand alone: its process tree showed what had started it, whether that was an application’s own process or a binary the attacker had planted.

The self-deleting binary is a good example: deleting the file does not stop the running program, so the sensor still recorded it as the parent of the commands that followed, which tied activity across many hosts back to the same tool.

From the sensor data, the research team rebuilt the attack from the first alert onward, decoded the attacker’s base64-encoded scripts, and mapped the containers and hosts involved.

One of the Node.js RCE alerts as it appeared in the Orca platform. The process tree shows the web app’s own Node.js process starting a shell that ran system recon commands as root. Identifying details and parts of the attacker’s commands are redacted.

How real-time detection shaped the incident response

Seeing the attack at an early stage shaped everything that followed. With those early and detailed alerts arriving in real time in the customer’s console, the research team used the same sensor data to piece the attack together as it unfolded, instead of working backward from a later alert. That meant they could reach out with the full picture while the attack was still in progress.

The customer confirmed that no red team or penetration test was running. The team shared a timeline built from the sensor’s alerts, along with the affected containers and hosts, the files the attacker dropped, the domain and address they used, the persistence they left behind (system services and auto-restarting containers), and which secrets may have been exposed, to help the customer’s team scope and contain the activity. Using that picture, the customer’s team contained the attack, removing the persistence and the attacker’s containers.

Runtime alerts live on the same platform as Orca’s cloud posture, identity, and vulnerability data. As a result, each alert appeared on the affected asset next to its exposure, vulnerabilities, and access, so the team saw the attack in full context in one place.

How to harden cloud workloads against similar attacks

A few practical steps make each stage of an attack like this harder:

Run web apps with least privilege. Run them as a non-root user, with a read-only filesystem where possible, so a compromised app can’t easily drop and run its own tools.

Limit access to the cloud metadata service. Block it for workloads that don’t need it, so a compromised container can’t collect cloud credentials.

Keep long-lived secrets out of environment variables and files. Prefer short-lived credentials and a secrets manager, so a shell in the app finds little worth stealing.

Block privileged containers and host namespace sharing. Allow them only where a workload truly needs them, and enforce that with policy rather than convention.

Restrict access to cluster control services. Limit which workloads can reach etcd and the kubelet API, and disable anonymous kubelet access, so a shell in one container can’t easily map or control the rest of the cluster.

Control outbound traffic. Let workloads reach only the destinations they need, which makes it much harder for an attacker to download tools or open a reverse shell.

Watch behavior, not just indicators. Activity that breaks a workload’s normal pattern, such as a web app starting shells or a container running a newly dropped binary, can expose an attack even when nothing known is involved. Alert on it, and for high-confidence detections, consider stopping it as it happens.

Detecting and stopping runtime attacks with Orca Sensor

Orca Sensor goes beyond known indicators: even when an attacker brings nothing known, their behavior gives them away. In this intrusion, the detections fired across the attack, from the exploited web app to recon and secret hunting, credential access, the break-out from containers to their hosts, and persistence. Seeing the attack never depended on a single alert, and together the alerts told the story of how it unfolded. Orca’s Threat Investigator Agent can reconstruct that story automatically from the alerts and their context. In alert mode, the sensor caught this attack. Set to terminate, the same detections that raised these alerts can stop the malicious processes as they run, not just flag them, including the Node.js RCE detections that fired before the attacker reached the host.

Title: PHP Patches 7 Critical Flaws, Including Session and PHP-FPM Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289)
Context: 0 (released with the fixes) These ranges apply to CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289 and most of the other vulnerabilities in the release; a few affect only some branches (see below)
Full Text:
On November 19, 2026, the PHP project released PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13, fixing 17 vulnerabilities. Seven are rated critical by the PHP project (CVSS 4.0 9.2), including CVE-2026-115560, a session serializer mismatch that can lead to remote code execution, and CVE-2026-129289, a PHP-FPM request smuggling flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker forge a backend request and execute attacker-controlled PHP code. PHP 8.6.0, released the same day, already includes the fixes.

PHP runs a large share of the world’s websites and web applications, in virtual machines, containers and managed platforms alike. CVE-2026-115560 was pre-announced in October, a few days after the PHP2Shell fixes (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), with the mitigation of disabling session upload progress. Today’s release publishes its full details and fixes it alongside 16 other vulnerabilities. Several of them need specific configurations, but the release as a whole affects every supported PHP branch.

PHP November 2026 security release: key facts

Fact

Detail

CVEs

17 in total; critical: CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474, CVE-2026-129182

Type

Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) in the session extension; HTTP request smuggling (CWE-444) in PHP-FPM; several use-after-free bugs

Severity

Rated critical by the PHP project (CVSS 4.0 9.2) for all seven; NVD score pending

Required configuration

CVE-2026-115560: session upload progress enabled and mismatched session serializers. CVE-2026-129289: PHP-FPM behind a front end that reuses FastCGI connections

Affected versions

PHP 8.2.0 to 8.2.35, 8.3.0 to 8.3.36, 8.4.0 to 8.4.27 and 8.5.0 to 8.5.12 (some CVEs affect only some branches)

Fixed versions

8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13; PHP 8.6.0 includes the fixes

Exposure

Internet-facing PHP applications; exploitability depends on configuration and on the application

Workaround

Set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 (CVE-2026-115560); disable FastCGI connection reuse on the front end (CVE-2026-129289); other CVEs have their own workarounds

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; a public proof of concept exists for CVE-2026-115560 in a lab setup

What is CVE-2026-115560?

CVE-2026-115560 is a flaw in PHP’s session upload progress feature. When a client uploads a file, PHP writes the upload’s progress into the user’s session, including a value the client controls. PHP supports several session serialization formats, and if that data is written in one format (php_serialize or php_binary) and later read in another (php), the reader can treat attacker-supplied bytes as serialized object data.

This can happen when an application switches session.serialize_handler at runtime before calling session_start(), or when separate applications, PHP-FPM pools, virtual hosts or command-line jobs with different settings share the same session storage. If the reading application has a suitable deserialization gadget chain, the attacker can execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker. According to the PHP advisory, the original report demonstrated command execution with a Guzzle gadget on PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and with a Monolog gadget.

The fix turns session upload progress off by default and blocks runtime changes to session settings while the feature is enabled. An explicit session.upload_progress.enabled = 1 in existing configuration still overrides the new default, and the PHP project notes that matching serializers across separate configurations is still the administrator’s responsibility.

What is CVE-2026-129289?

CVE-2026-129289 is an HTTP request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM. When an application opens php://input but does not read the request body to the end, PHP can leave the unread bytes on a persistent FastCGI connection. An attacker can place a crafted FastCGI message in that body, and PHP-FPM accepts it as a new request that the web server never created or authorized.

The forged request controls FastCGI parameters, including the script to run and administrator-level PHP settings, which lets the attacker execute attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker in a single unauthenticated request, provided they know the path of an existing PHP script on the server. According to the PHP advisory, no non-default PHP setting, memory corruption or race condition is needed, and the bug has existed since PHP 5.6.0.

Exploitation requires a front end that reuses backend connections, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy FastCGI applications that keep connections open. Standard nginx and Apache configurations that close the FastCGI connection after each request are not affected by the demonstrated attack. LSAPI is affected by the same cleanup bug, but the advisory does not establish code execution through LSAPI.

These ranges apply to CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289 and most of the other vulnerabilities in the release; a few affect only some branches (see below). PHP 8.1 and older are end of life and received no release, although the PHP project notes that older versions may also be affected (session upload progress was introduced in PHP 5.4.0). Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number, so check your distribution’s security tracker as well as the version string. PHP bundled in container images and application platforms needs its own update.

Additional vulnerabilities fixed in the same release

The other five critical vulnerabilities (all CVSS 4.0 9.2 according to the PHP project):

CVE-2026-126714 (8.2 to 8.5): partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution. Requires attacker influence over session data, an interrupted write and a gadget chain. Disabling session upload progress removes one input path but is not a full fix.

CVE-2026-129496 (8.2 to 8.5): a timezone cache use-after-free can lead to remote code execution. Requires a startup diagnostic and PHP error logging to a file; code execution was demonstrated locally in PHP-FPM and Apache mod_php under additional assumptions.

CVE-2026-129481 (8.3 to 8.5): use-after-free after an interrupted session shutdown. Code execution has not been demonstrated. Disabling session upload progress does not address it.

CVE-2026-129474 (8.5 only): use-after-free in magic method backtraces can lead to remote code execution, confirmed by the PHP project on PHP 8.5. It depends on the application and requires bypassing address randomization.

CVE-2026-129182 (8.5 only): use-after-free in the fatal error backtrace after shutdown. Code execution through this path has not been demonstrated.

The release also fixes four high-severity issues: a PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free that allows local privilege escalation to root when the FPM master runs as root (CVE-2026-129291, affecting configurations with catch_workers_output enabled, including the official PHP-FPM Docker images), a denial of service through folded HTTP response headers (CVE-2026-127960), mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs that can send data in plaintext (CVE-2026-128064), and a PHAR signature bypass (CVE-2026-128090). Six medium-severity issues affect PHP-CGI, SOAP, DOM, the URI extension and the PHP-FPM status page.

Is there a patch for CVE-2026-115560 and CVE-2026-129289?

Yes. PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13 were released on November 19, 2026 and are available on the PHP downloads page. PHP 8.6.0, released the same day, includes the same fixes. Linux distributions, container image maintainers and hosting platforms that ship PHP need to release their own updated packages.

How to mitigate the PHP vulnerabilities

The best fix is to upgrade to the fixed release for your branch. Each critical vulnerability has a different workaround, and no single setting covers all of them.

Inventory: find every PHP installation, including PHP in container images, PHP-FPM pools and application platforms, and note which ones run PHP-FPM behind nginx, Apache or HAProxy.

Upgrade: move to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0, then restart the PHP master process and all workers.

CVE-2026-115560: set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the FPM pool configuration. Calling ini_set() from the application is too late. Check for explicit settings that re-enable it, even after upgrading.

CVE-2026-129289: disable FastCGI connection reuse: leave nginx fastcgi_keep_conn off, leave Apache enablereuse off, or configure other front ends to close the backend connection after each request. Never expose PHP-FPM listeners to untrusted networks.

CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 (PHP 8.5): set zend.exception_ignore_args = 1 or fatal_error_backtraces = 0.

CVE-2026-129496: fix configuration errors that produce startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a log file.

CVE-2026-129291: disable catch_workers_output in affected FPM pools, and avoid running the FPM master as root where possible.

Prioritize internet-facing PHP-FPM servers behind connection-reusing front ends, and applications that share session storage or change session settings at runtime.

Is CVE-2026-115560 being exploited in the wild?

There are no known reports of in-the-wild exploitation of any of the vulnerabilities, and none is listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. A public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2026-115560 has been available on GitHub since October, but it targets a deliberately vulnerable lab application with a built-in gadget. With full technical details for all 17 vulnerabilities now public, especially for the PHP-FPM request smuggling flaw, exploit attempts are likely to follow.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable PHP versions, including PHP installed from OS packages and PHP bundled in container images, and to understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, so they can prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone.

Title: Quantum deadlines are here. Meet Orca’s new tools for PQC readiness.
Context: Building on the PQC compliance framework we launched in July, Orca now gives teams a live inventory of their cryptography, a clear read on how exposed each key and certificate...
Full Text:
Post-quantum deadlines are no longer a distant line on a roadmap. US federal agencies owed their PQC migration plans in October. High-value federal systems must move key establishment to post-quantum cryptography by the end of 2030. And the EU expects member states to start cryptographic inventories by the end of this year, with contractors, regulated industries, and their suppliers next in line.

Yet the first step is still where most teams stall. Knowing RSA and ECC have to go tells you nothing about where they run in your cloud, which of those assets face the internet, what data they protect, or what breaks if you change them. Without those answers, teams either try to boil the ocean with a spreadsheet inventory or let PQC sit in the backlog until the next audit.

The cloud makes this harder than most environments. Cryptography is spread across managed key services, load balancers, certificates, SSH keys, VPN tunnels, container images, and code, and it changes every time someone deploys. A spreadsheet inventory is out of date the day it’s finished.

That’s why we’re expanding Orca’s post-quantum cryptography capabilities. Building on the PQC compliance framework we launched in July, Orca now gives teams a live inventory of their cryptography, a clear read on how exposed each key and certificate is to quantum attacks, and one place to track readiness. This post covers what’s new, then shows it in action on a real example.

What’s new in Orca for post-quantum cryptography

Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM). See every key, certificate, key pair, and cryptography library across your cloud in one live inventory. CBOM shows algorithms, key lengths, and expiration dates for cloud keys and vaults, the SSH keys and key files sitting on your workloads, and the crypto packages they run. Export it in CycloneDX for auditors, customers, and GRC tools.

PQC Impact. Know at a glance which cryptography quantum computing will break. Each key and certificate is rated Vulnerable, Weakened, or Resistant based on its algorithm and key length, so you can filter and group your inventory by quantum risk instead of decoding algorithm names.

Title: Breaking: “ruby2ßhell” or ruby2shell One-Byte Heap Overflow in Ruby Could Allow Remote Code Execution in Rails and Popular Self-Hosted Apps
Context: The Ruby core team rates the issue critical and states that changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution, adding that it is aware of proof-of-concept...
Full Text:
A heap-based buffer overflow in Ruby’s string case conversion, tracked as CVE-2026-132825 and dubbed “ruby2ßhell”, has been disclosed. The Ruby core team rates the issue critical and states that changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution, adding that it is aware of proof-of-concept exploits that can trigger code execution in some scenarios. Fixed versions, Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10, were released on November 18, 2026.

Ruby powers a large number of web applications and widely used self-hosted platforms. According to the researchers who published the ruby2ßhell write-up, the flaw is reachable without authentication in default Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications, as well as in self-hosted software such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon and Discourse. The vulnerable code has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. The same Ruby release also fixes six additional memory-safety vulnerabilities in Ruby’s regular expression engine and string case conversion.

ruby2ßhell (CVE-2026-132825): key facts

Fact

Detail

CVE

CVE-2026-132825 (GitHub advisory GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5)

Type

One-byte heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122 / CWE-193) in string case conversion

Severity

Rated critical by the Ruby core team; NVD score pending

Trigger

Changing the case (e.g., upcase) of a crafted string in certain single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252; UTF-8 strings are not affected

Affected Ruby versions

3.3.13 and earlier; 3.4.0 to 3.4.12; 4.0.0 to 4.0.9 (end-of-life versions back to 2.4.0, according to the researchers)

Fixed Ruby versions

3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10 (released November 18, 2026)

Exposure

According to the researchers: reachable without authentication in default Rails and classic-style Sinatra apps, and in GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, Discourse and other self-hosted software

Workaround

None published; upgrade Ruby (and self-hosted software that bundles Ruby)

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; the Ruby team is aware of non-public PoCs, and the researchers plan to publish a PoC about a week after disclosure

What is ruby2ßhell (CVE-2026-132825)?

The flaw is in how Ruby converts the case of strings in several single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1, ISO-8859-2 and other ISO-8859 variants, and Windows-1250, Windows-1252, Windows-1254 and Windows-1257. In these encodings, the German sharp s (“ß”, byte 0xDF) becomes two characters (“SS”) when upper-cased, but Ruby checked for only one byte of room in the output buffer. A crafted string containing enough of these characters makes Ruby write one byte past the end of a heap buffer. The researchers note that the issue can be reached through upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?, while UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Although the overflow is only a single byte, heap memory corruption of this kind can be leveraged for code execution. The Ruby core team states that it is aware of PoCs that use the flaw to trigger remote code execution in some scenarios. The Ruby team rates the advisory critical, and the researchers describe unauthenticated remote exposure in common frameworks; organizations should treat internet-facing Ruby applications as at risk.

Which Ruby versions are affected?

Ruby branch

Affected versions

Fixed version

Ruby 4.0

4.0.0 to 4.0.9

4.0.10

Ruby 3.4

3.4.0 to 3.4.12

3.4.13

Ruby 3.3

3.3.13 and earlier

3.3.14

Ruby 3.2 and earlier

Affected (back to 2.4.0, according to the researchers)

No fix: end of life, upgrade to a supported branch

Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive these fixes. Ruby is often bundled inside applications and container images, so self-hosted platforms (such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, Discourse, OpenProject and Chatwoot, which the researchers list as affected in their latest versions at the time of disclosure) need their own vendor updates. Linux distributions may ship the fix as a patched package without changing the Ruby version number, so check the relevant distribution advisory.

Additional Ruby vulnerabilities fixed in the same release

Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10 fix seven vulnerabilities in total. Besides ruby2ßhell, the release addresses six other memory-safety flaws. The Ruby team says it is aware of proof-of-concept exploits proving remote code execution for five of the seven vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-132825. At the time of writing, these are tracked by GitHub advisory IDs, as CVE identifiers had not yet been assigned:

GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px (high): integer overflow in string case conversion leading to a heap buffer overflow.

GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x (critical): double free in regular expression compilation, relevant to applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns.

GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w (critical): heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation.

GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4 (high): heap buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s.

GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r (high): out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching.

GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h (medium): out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching, which may disclose memory or crash the process.

Upgrading to a fixed Ruby version addresses all seven vulnerabilities.

Is there a patch for CVE-2026-132825?

Yes. The Ruby core team released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 on November 18, 2026, and strongly recommends upgrading. The fix ensures that two bytes of output space are available when the sharp s is converted. Self-hosted software and container images that bundle Ruby need to be updated or rebuilt once their vendors ship versions based on the fixed Ruby releases.

How to mitigate ruby2ßhell

No official workaround has been published; upgrading Ruby is the fix. Recommended steps:

Inventory all Ruby runtimes, including OS packages, Ruby installed via version managers or tarballs, Ruby bundled inside self-hosted applications, and container images.

Upgrade to Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10, and move applications running end-of-life Ruby versions (3.2 and earlier) to a supported branch. These are fixes to the Ruby interpreter itself, not to a gem, so updating gems (for example with bundle update) does not address them.

Update self-hosted platforms such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon and Discourse as soon as their vendors release fixed versions, and rebuild container images on patched base images.

Prioritize internet-facing Rails and Sinatra applications and other Ruby services that process untrusted input.

Is ruby2ßhell being exploited in the wild?

At the time of writing, there are no reports of in-the-wild exploitation. The Ruby core team states that it is aware of proof-of-concept exploits that can trigger remote code execution in some scenarios, but these have not been published. The researchers behind the ruby2ßhell write-up have said they plan to publish a proof of concept about a week after disclosure, which is likely to accelerate exploitation attempts. Given how widely Ruby is used in internet-facing applications, organizations should treat this vulnerability as urgent.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable Ruby versions, including Ruby installed from OS packages and Ruby bundled in container images, and to understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, so they can prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone.

Title: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI Supply-Chain Attack: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 Steal Cloud Credentials
Context: A critical supply-chain compromise was discovered affecting Microsoft’s agent-framework PyPI meta-package, where versions 1
Full Text:
A critical supply-chain compromise was discovered affecting Microsoft’s agent-framework PyPI meta-package, where versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were injected with credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud identity tokens, API keys, and sensitive credentials from developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, and cloud build hosts. Due to the package’s approximately 190,000 monthly downloads and the breadth of targeted credentials, immediate remediation is required for any environment that installed the compromised versions.

Agent-framework compromise at a glance

Affected package: agent-framework on PyPI, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2

Last clean version: 1.26.0

Not affected: agent-framework-core and 22 other sibling packages

Exposure window: November 17, 2026, 20:35 to approximately 21:20 UTC

Payload: a Python .pth startup hook that harvests credentials on every interpreter launch

Exfiltration: zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook.site URL

Status: malicious versions quarantined by PyPI; no CVE assigned

What happened in the agent-framework supply-chain attack

Both malicious versions were published within a 33-minute window on November 17, 2026 (20:35 to 21:08 UTC) and removed by approximately 21:20 UTC.

The attack was entirely in packaging. Neither malicious release changed Agent Framework code or pulled in a rogue dependency. Instead, each version added a Python .pth startup hook file that executes on every Python interpreter launch, even if Agent Framework is never imported.

How the .pth startup hook runs and evades detection

The collector forks a detached background process, sets a flag to prevent re-execution in child processes, and silently harvests credentials. Version 1.26.2 restored the legitimate __init__.py byte-for-byte to evade diff-based detection while moving the payload to a new top-level module.

What credentials does the agent-framework malware steal?

The malware actively requested fresh credential tokens rather than only copying stored secrets. Targeted credentials include:

Environment variables matching sensitive substrings (TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, and more) from the current process and up to 300 other processes via /proc/*/environ

Azure managed-identity tokens for 12 Azure resources (ARM, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, ML, AI Foundry, Container Registry, Azure DevOps) via IMDS and identity endpoints

Azure DevOps SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and OIDC tokens for federated identity

GitHub Actions OIDC tokens (version 1.26.2 only) when workflows have id-token: write permissions

Credential files including Azure CLI state, .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config.json, Hugging Face tokens, and .env files

All harvested data was exfiltrated via zlib-compressed, base64-encoded JSON posted to a webhook.site URL.

Which agent-framework versions and environments are affected?

The following components are affected: agent-framework versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on PyPI. The last clean version is 1.26.0. The dependency agent-framework-core and 22 other sibling packages were checked and are not affected.

Any environment that installed the compromised versions during the exposure window is at risk, including through loose version pins such as agent-framework>=1.26. This spans developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines (Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions), and cloud build hosts running Python.

At the time of writing, the malicious versions have been quarantined by PyPI and the Microsoft publisher account has been secured. No CVE has been assigned.

Why stolen cloud and CI/CD credentials raise the stakes

Successful exploitation allows attackers to obtain cloud identity tokens that grant access to Azure resources, steal CI/CD pipeline secrets that could enable lateral movement across repositories and infrastructure, and harvest stored credentials that could lead to full infrastructure compromise across multiple cloud providers.

The attack also demonstrates sophisticated evasion techniques, including restoring legitimate code to bypass diff-based reviews while hiding the payload in a separate module.

How to remediate the agent-framework compromise

Organizations should take the following remediation steps immediately:

Isolate affected hosts and CI runners.

Detect exposure by searching lockfiles, container images, CI caches, and environments for versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, and look for .pth files (agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth) and payload modules in site-packages.

Pin to agent-framework==1.26.0 with hash verification and rebuild from clean environments.

Rotate all credentials that may have been exposed, including Azure service principal credentials, Azure DevOps PATs and service connections, GitHub tokens, npm/PyPI/Hugging Face tokens, Docker registry credentials, and any secrets in environment variables or .env files.

Audit Azure Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure DevOps audit logs, and GitHub Actions workflow runs for unauthorized access since November 17.

Hunt for IOCs by searching proxy and DNS logs for connections to webhook.site, User-Agent strings “af-runtime-diagnostics/1” and “runtime-diagnostics/1”, and bursts of IMDS token requests.

Block versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 at your package proxy and consider blocking webhook.site at the network level.

Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

Package versions: agent-framework 1.26.1, 1.26.2

Files in site-packages: agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth

Network: outbound connections to webhook.site

User-Agent strings: “af-runtime-diagnostics/1”, “runtime-diagnostics/1”

Behavior: bursts of IMDS token requests

How Orca helps detect compromised agent-framework packages

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable package versions, understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability, and asset criticality, and prioritize the risks that matter most. Orca’s SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scanning capabilities can detect compromised packages in cloud workloads. Customers running Orca’s agentless scanning should check whether their workloads contain the affected versions. Orca’s platform highlights affected assets directly, helping security teams focus on the most critical remediation paths first.

Because this payload targets build hosts and pipelines as much as production, coverage has to start before deployment. Orca helps teams catch risky code before it reaches production. And because the real damage comes from what stolen tokens can reach, Orca also helps teams reduce identity-based cloud risk and detect and respond to cloud threats that follow a credential compromise. As agent frameworks become a recurring supply-chain target, securing AI systems means securing the packages they are built on.

Title: Two Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws Could Allow Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
Context: The vulnerabilities were discovered independently by several research teams and reported to F5, which released fixed versions on November 18, 2026
Full Text:
F5 has disclosed two critical vulnerabilities in NGINX, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both in the HTTP/2 module (ngx_http_v2_module). Both are rated 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 (8.1 under CVSS 3.1) and can be triggered remotely without authentication on NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled. Successful exploitation can crash NGINX worker processes, corrupt memory and potentially lead to remote code execution on the server.

NGINX is one of the most widely deployed web servers and reverse proxies, often sitting in front of multiple websites and APIs. Because the flaws are in NGINX itself, applications behind an affected NGINX instance can be exposed even when their own code is secure. One of the flaws, CVE-2026-123007, dates back to NGINX 1.9.5, released in 2015. The vulnerabilities were discovered independently by several research teams and reported to F5, which released fixed versions on November 18, 2026.

NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities: key facts

Fact

Detail

CVEs

CVE-2026-123633 (use-after-free, CWE-416); CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow leading to heap buffer overflow, CWE-191 / CWE-787)

Severity

CVSS 4.0: 9.2 (Critical); CVSS 3.1: 8.1 (High) for both

Component

NGINX HTTP/2 module (ngx_http_v2_module)

Attack

Remote, unauthenticated, no user interaction

Required configuration

HTTP/2 enabled. CVE-2026-123633 additionally requires NGINX to proxy requests to a backend and the worker process to be running low on worker_connections

Affected NGINX Open Source

CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 and later; CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 and later (up to the fixed releases below)

Fixed NGINX Open Source

1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline)

Affected / fixed NGINX Plus

R33 and later; fixed in 37.0.8.1 and 37.3.0.1 (see version table below)

Workaround

Disable HTTP/2 until patched

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; public proof-of-concept code for CVE-2026-123007 is available

What are CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007?

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety flaws in how NGINX processes HTTP/2 traffic.

CVE-2026-123633 (HTTP/2 connection use-after-free). NGINX keeps a list of idle connections that it may close when it runs out of free connection slots. An HTTP/2 connection could remain on this “reusable” list even after a new request stream started on it. When NGINX is proxying the request to a backend and is running low on worker_connections, it can close and free that connection while the request is still using it, resulting in a use-after-free in the worker process. The fix resets the connection’s reusable status when a new stream is created.

CVE-2026-123007 (HTTP/2 flow-control integer underflow). When an HTTP/2 stream is terminated, its unsent data is credited back to the connection’s flow-control window. A client could cause this window to exceed its allowed maximum, which breaks NGINX’s buffer size accounting and leads to an out-of-bounds memory write (heap buffer overflow), typically followed by a worker crash. Unlike CVE-2026-123633, this flaw does not require a backend: according to the researchers, it can also affect NGINX instances that only serve static content over HTTP/2. The fix accounts for queued frames when validating the client’s WINDOW_UPDATE.

According to F5, both flaws can lead to denial of service and memory corruption, and code execution is possible on systems where Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is disabled or can be bypassed. Researchers who reported the issues state that they were able to achieve code execution, including bypassing ASLR, on standard 64-bit systems. Both issues affect the data plane only; F5 reports no control-plane exposure.

Which NGINX versions are affected?

Any NGINX deployment with HTTP/2 enabled that runs an affected version should be considered vulnerable. Versions on branches that have reached End of Technical Support are not evaluated by F5; they should be upgraded to a supported fixed release.

Product

CVE

Affected versions

Fixed versions

NGINX Open Source

CVE-2026-123633

1.19.7 and later, including 1.30.0 to 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 to 1.31.8

1.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline)

NGINX Open Source

CVE-2026-123007

1.9.5 and later, including 1.30.0 to 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 to 1.31.8

1.30.7 (stable), 1.31.9 (mainline)

NGINX Plus

CVE-2026-123633
